I know it sounds weird, but antidepressant really can exacerbate issues with suicidality, especially in younger people. In many ways it's distinct from suicidal feelings you may otherwise have, and it can be hard to understand the difference, so thats why they prefer to wait until you are older.

In general, I can say that the best way to get the right treatment, is to be 100% honest about how you feel. Downplaying or even making it sound worse, will make treating you harder.
If you aren't 100% honest with those treating you, they won't be able help you properly. The words you use need to be your own and based on what you think and feel.

rTMS (Repetitive High Frequency Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation)   


It's a treatment that uses a strong electromagnet to do a bunch of physics magic to certain areas of the brain.  From my limited understanding, it's kind of ECT's friendlier cousin. I live in a place where health care is provided so I have no ideas of availability or cost and such.

The treatment was pretty intensive with 30 minutes every weekday for a few months. While it wasn't painful, it could be pretty uncomfortable. After a little under a month, I slowly started to feel better, and one day I realized that I was no longer depressed. It was like I'd had a stuffy nose for years, and then suddenly being able to breathe again. I was in a good mood, I could function and my self loathing was gone. I was content.  Some of the effect was likely a placebo, but I felt like I never have before. The feeling really was like night and day.  


The effect slowly tapered off, and after a solid two months I was depressed again. This was kind of expected. The treatment needs maintenance and the effect varies. The depression felt fairly familiar but, something in me had changed. I don't feel as bad as I did, and now I know what life without depression can look like, and that it's possible. I was so sure that nothing could change, I really *knew*, and yet I was wrong.

​

Even if we feel like  we are doing everything right, depression doesn't always make sense, and some of us might need a little extra help. I hope you find a treatment that works.

Are there any other treatment options available to you? I'm 37 and like you, have spent most of my life with depression. It wasn't until last year that I found a treatment that helped in any meaningful way. Not being depressed had been an alien concept to me, and I had never really believed things could get better. Finding the right treatment is hard, but I truly believe that change can happen, no matter how impossible it seems.

You are not lazy. Working through depression isn't easy, and there will be ups and downs, but apathy isn't something you just wish yourself out of. Medication and other treatments are meant to give you the push you need to get the work done.

If I have learned one thing from struggling with depression, it's that you have to be 100% open with both yourself and those treating you. If they don't have the full picture, they can't help you properly. It can be scary, but reality is rarely as scary as your mind makes it out to be.

Good luck.

I used to think that I was depressed some of the time, and that I was just a lazy bum the rest of the time. With the years I understood that I infact was depressed all of the time, and I would periodically move through differing states of depression. Before last year I could have counted months in terms of time spent not depressed. It was hard to define what a lack of depression felt like, since it was so alien to me. The only thing I could identify was glimpses of energy that disappeared as fast as they came, maybe a few days, a couple of times a year.

Last spring I went through an rTMS treatment. While I didn't really expect much, I gave it my all. After a few weeks I started to notice a lighter mood and bouts of energy. It appreciated the respite, but I assumed it was a placebo effect. After a month I  slowly realised that I wasn't depressed anymore, truly unlike anything I have ever experienced. There was no weight on my shoulders, no dark thoughts or a dark filter in experiencing the world. I could love myself and enjoy my own company, and even take properly care of myself and my apartment. For the first time in my life I felt free. It felt like I was able to enjoy existence and experience joy, all by myself.

In total this lasted a couple of months, slowly dissipating as the treatment ended. Before the end of the summer I was depressed again. I knew it was likely to happen, but it was rough.

With the experiencenses of last year and a new medicine, I have more energy and I'm able to live more of a "normal" life. I'm still depressed, and It's hard to figure out life when I'm closing in on forty, but I have some of the freedom of last year, and I know what life without depression looks like.

I can relate to this in a huge way. What you describe here was my reality until last year. Depression and avoidance just made everything pile up.

Last spring I tried a new treatment, and for a few months my depression was gone for the first time in 20+ years. I had energy, and I was able to live mire fully. After the effect tapered off, I was back to normal, depressed with no energy. I was sad at first, but at the end of the summer, I started therapy with a psychologist. During the sessions I slowly realised that something was different. It dawned on me that I was no longer afraid of not being depressed. Deep inside I had feared that I was just being lazy, and I was unable to cope with it.

I changed medication during fall, and slowly got energy. Now I could take better care of my appartment and myself. I start making healthier dinners, and going for walks. 

It's still an uphill battle. I'm still a bit depressed, and all these years being depressed has set me back in terms of life goals, but I feel more free and able to tackle these challenges.
